evals.name: java-write-late-fees
evals.prompt: Write a JUnit 5 test suite for the library circulation module in evals/files/java/write-late-fees (Maven, Java 21; JUnit Jupiter, AssertJ and Mockito are already in the pom). Its entry point is CirculationService (checkOut / returnBook); the Javadoc on CirculationService and LateFeePolicy is the authoritative contract. There are no tests yet. Leave production code unchanged. Decide which collaborators should be real, faked or mocked, and explain why. Run the suite with `mvn -o test`, then show that it catches a plausible defect by mutating production code in a disposable copy (not the original). Save the test sources, the mutated copy, and a short report (the test portfolio and why, commands run, test results, the mutation and which test caught it) under outputs/java-write-late-fees/.
evals.expected_output: A small honeycomb-shaped suite. Most tests drive CirculationService.checkOut/returnBook end to end with a real FileLoanStore on a @TempDir, an injected fixed or controllable java.time.Clock, and a mock or recording fake of only MemberNotifier. Fee boundaries are covered by a named-row parameterized table, either a unit table on LateFeePolicy.feeCents or a slice table through checkOut/returnBook with an offset clock. The suite is green offline, and a disposable mutation (for example a grace-boundary or cap-order change) is caught by a behavioral assertion.
expectations: Most feature tests enter through CirculationService (checkOut then returnBook) with real in-process wiring (real LateFeePolicy, real FileLoanStore). They assert on the ReturnReceipt and on the persisted Loan read back through the store (returnedOn, feeCents).

No test targets trivial records such as Loan, ReturnReceipt or LateFeeNotice. Any test that targets FileLoanStore on its own is an integration test against a real @TempDir (a few are acceptable for behavior awkward to reach through CirculationService); none uses a mocked store.

Fee boundaries are covered by a parameterized table (@CsvSource/@MethodSource) with a readable name per row, either a unit table on LateFeePolicy.feeCents or a slice table through checkOut/returnBook with an offset clock (more than one table is fine if row shapes differ). The rows cover on-time/early (0), 2 days late (0, grace), 3 days (75), 7 days (175), 8 days (225), a STUDENT half-rounded-up case (e.g. 3 days -> 38), and the replacement-cost cap. At least one literal-valued row intersects the student discount and the cap so that applying the cap before the discount fails it (e.g. STUDENT, 10 days late, replacement cost 200 -> 163; capping first would give 100); separate student and cap rows alone do not satisfy this. There are no copy-pasted one-case-per-method fee tests, and no loops or conditionals in test bodies that select the scenario or compute an expected value (the parameterized runner, assertion-only checks and fail-fast guards are fine).
If unit-level tests exist, they target only LateFeePolicy; CirculationService orchestration is never unit-tested with doubles.

Every test that goes through CirculationService uses a real FileLoanStore on a JUnit @TempDir (no in-memory LoanStore fake). LoanStore and LateFeePolicy are never Mockito mocks, and no test uses when(...).thenReturn on them.

MemberNotifier is the only test double that verifies interactions (Mockito mock/verify or a recording fake). Tests check the exact LateFeeNotice (to, loanId, daysLate, feeCents) for a late return, and check that no notice is sent when the fee is 0 (on time or within grace).

Time is controlled by passing a Clock.fixed/offset or a mutable test Clock into CirculationService, with a zone set explicitly. Nothing calls Thread.sleep or depends on the system clock or today's date.

Through the entry point, the suite covers the contract's non-happy paths: when MemberNotifier throws NotificationFailedException the return is still persisted and the receipt has noticeSent == false; a second returnBook on the same loan throws IllegalStateException; an unknown loan id throws UnknownLoanException. The documented ordering (the return is persisted before the e-mail is attempted) is checked through observable state: a notifier fake or Mockito answer that, when invoked, reads the loan from the real FileLoanStore and asserts (or records for a later assertion) that returnedOn and feeCents are already persisted, so moving store.save after the notification attempt fails a test.
Test names describe behavior (e.g. returnWithinGracePeriodChargesNothing), not method names or numbers.
The suite passes under `mvn -o test` against the unchanged production code (JUnit 5.9.2 as pinned; no pom version bump).

A plausible, observable production mutation (e.g. `late <= GRACE_DAYS` changed to `<`, the student discount applied after the cap together with a STUDENT cap row, or the fee persisted as 0) is applied only in a disposable copy, and at least one named behavioral test is shown to fail on it.
The original fixture stays unmodified (no production edits, no test files written into it).

evals.name: java-refactor-order-suite
evals.prompt: Our order-placement service in evals/files/java/refactor-order-placement (Maven, Java 21, JUnit 5 + Mockito) has a passing test suite that keeps breaking whenever we refactor, and we still had a production bug slip through. First review the existing tests in src/test/java and give a concrete findings list: file/test name, what is wrong, and why it matters. Then refactor the suite to fix those problems. Keep production code unchanged; if you really need a seam, add the smallest one and say why. The suite must stay green with `mvn -o test`. Save the refactored tests, the findings list, and a short summary of the new test portfolio and what it now covers under outputs/java-refactor-order-suite/.
evals.expected_output: A findings list that names the planted problems: OrderService tests that mock managed/in-process collaborators and verify interactions, including the call-order test that breaks under a behavior-preserving refactor; stub-echo assertions; reflection on private roundHalfEven; copy-pasted testPricing1-5; loop/conditional logic; test1-style names; Thread.sleep with the system clock; and the uncovered payment-declined path. The suite is rebuilt as a few slice tests through OrderController.placeOrder with real OrderService, PricingCalculator, InMemoryInventory and InMemoryOrderRepository, a fixed Clock, deterministic ids, and only PaymentGateway doubled, plus one named-row parameterized table for PricingCalculator.quote. It stays green, and production code is unchanged because the Clock and id seams already exist.
expectations: The findings identify OrderServiceTest.testPlaceOrder (InOrder over available/reserve/unitPriceCents/quote/charge/save) and testChecksAvailabilityFirst (times(1) on inventory.available) as implementation-coupled. They explain that a behavior-preserving refactor, such as dropping the redundant available() pre-check because reserve() already returns false, would break them.

The findings identify the missing behavior: no test covers a declined payment (PaymentDeclinedException). Nothing checks that reserved stock is released, that no order is saved, or that OrderController returns 402. The refactored suite adds a test through the entry point asserting the 402 response, unchanged stock in InMemoryInventory, and no order in InMemoryOrderRepository.

The findings flag OrderServiceTest.testTotal: it verifies the stubbed query pricing.quote (an assertion on a stub), and it replaces the in-process PricingCalculator with a stub (inappropriate substitution), so its 5400 total assertion checks only propagation of the canned quote and never exercises the real discount calculation. Crediting the total assertion with catching propagation bugs is correct; the replacement suite keeps a total assertion against the real PricingCalculator.

The findings flag the OrderControllerTest tests that mock OrderService (e.g. testPlaceOrderWorks asserting totalCents 1234 taken straight from the stub) as tests that mock an in-process managed collaborator and so give limited protection: some assertions only echo stubbed values (totalCents 1234), the verify(service).place calls couple them to the implementation, and the 402 mapping is untested. Do not require claiming that every assertion echoes the stub; the 201/409 status assertions do check the controller's own mapping, and saying so is correct.

The refactored suite has no verify/when-then assertions on stubs, and no stubs of in-process or managed collaborators whose canned values the tests assert. Asserting that the persisted Order carries the paymentId returned by the PaymentGateway fake is allowed.
The findings flag PricingCalculatorTest.testRounding (reflection on private roundHalfEven) and the direct bulkDiscountPercent checks as implementation-detail testing.
The findings flag testPricing1-5 as copy-pasted cases and testManyQuantities as logic in a test (a loop with if/else that re-implements the tiers).
The findings flag test1/testPricingN as vague names and testTimestamp as relying on Thread.sleep with Clock.systemUTC().

Findings carry severities consistent with the skill's review checklist: assertions on stubs and mocked managed dependencies (so real bugs pass) are high; call-count/call-order verification, reflection or private-member access, and sleeps with the real clock are at least medium; vague names and copy-paste are low.

Honeycomb portfolio after the refactor: feature behavior (201 with the correct discounted total, 400 validation including the 500 upper bound, 409 out of stock, 402 declined) is tested through OrderController.placeOrder with a real OrderService, PricingCalculator, InMemoryInventory and InMemoryOrderRepository. The fine-grained mocked OrderControllerTest/OrderServiceTest unit tests are removed or consolidated, and no test mocks OrderService, InventoryRepository, OrderRepository or PricingCalculator.

PaymentGateway is the only collaborator replaced by a mock or fake (it is unmanaged and third-party). At least one slice test asserts the recorded charge: card token, amount equal to the response's discounted totalCents, and idempotency key equal to the order id. The out-of-stock (409) and validation (400) paths assert that no charge was made.

Unit tests are kept only for PricingCalculator.quote, through its public method. They use one @ParameterizedTest with named rows covering the 9/10 and 49/50 tier boundaries, WELCOME10 including the never-below-zero floor, and half-even rounding ties in both directions through quote (for example unit price 5 x quantity 10 gives discount 2, which HALF_UP would make 3, and unit price 7 x quantity 10 gives discount 4). There is no reflection and no call to bulkDiscountPercent.

Time and ids are made deterministic through the existing constructor seams (Clock.fixed and a fixed Supplier<String>), with no Thread.sleep. The coverage of the old testSavesOrder is kept, not dropped: after a successful placeOrder, a test reads the order back through the real InMemoryOrderRepository (find with the fixed id, or findByCustomer) and asserts its customerId, its line (sku, quantity and unit price), the paymentId returned by the PaymentGateway fake, totalCents equal to the discounted total, and placedAt equal to the fixed clock instant. Asserting only on the PlaceOrderResponse does not satisfy this, because a wrong customer or empty paymentId would still be persisted unnoticed.
Production code is left unchanged (the answer notes that no new seam was needed), and `mvn -o test` passes.

Replacement tests are shown to catch a defect, not just claimed to: the answer gives a concrete production mutation applied only in a disposable copy (e.g. the stock release on PaymentDeclinedException removed, a tier boundary `>=` changed to `>`, or the WELCOME10 floor dropped), the exact command run against that copy (e.g. `mvn -o test` in the copy), and the name of the new behavioral test that failed. A bare statement that the new suite would catch it does not satisfy this.

evals.name: go-write-checkout-suite
evals.prompt: Write a test suite for the Go package in evals/files/go/write-checkout (package checkout: pricing, an in-memory store, a checkout service and an HTTP handler). The doc comments are the authoritative contract. Use only the standard library testing tools (no testify, gomock or other third-party modules) and leave production code unchanged. Run the suite. Then show that it catches a plausible defect: apply one realistic production mutation in a disposable copy of the module (never the original) and show which test fails. Save the test file(s), the mutated copy and a short report under outputs/go-write-checkout/. The report should list the commands and results, the mutation, and which dependencies are real and which are replaced (and why).
evals.expected_output: A mostly slice-level Go suite: httptest-driven POST /orders (or Service.Checkout) tests with real NewMemoryStore wiring, a spy only for ReceiptSender, an injected Now/NewID, and one named-row table test for PriceOrder boundaries. The suite passes, and a mutation in a disposable copy is shown to be caught.
expectations: `go test ./...` passes against the unchanged production files, and go.mod gains no require lines (stdlib testing only: no testify, gomock or similar).

Honeycomb portfolio: most tests drive a feature entry point (NewHandler via httptest POST /orders, or Service.Checkout) wired to a real NewMemoryStore. Together they cover at least these outcomes: success (totals, stock decremented, order persisted); insufficient stock; unknown SKU or unknown/expired coupon; invalid request (e.g. empty items, qty <= 0 or an email without '@'); and duplicate SKUs merged before pricing. At least one test (a table is fine) goes through NewHandler with httptest and asserts the status mapping: 201 on success, 400 for malformed JSON or an invalid request, 409 for insufficient stock and 422 for an unknown SKU or coupon. Outcomes tested only through Service.Checkout assert the returned error (errors.Is on the sentinel), not a status. Quantity validation is covered separately from the other invalid-request cases: named zero-quantity (qty 0) and negative-quantity (e.g. qty -2) cases go through Service.Checkout or NewHandler with a real NewMemoryStore and each asserts errors.Is(err, ErrInvalidRequest) (or 400 through NewHandler), the product's literal stock unchanged via store.Product (e.g. still 10), no stored order (store.Order for the injected NewID returns ErrNotFound) and no receipt recorded by the ReceiptSender spy. Deleting the `it.Qty <= 0` guard in Checkout must make these checks fail (without it, qty 0 creates an order and qty -2 increases stock and creates an order). Empty items, an email without '@' or malformed JSON alone do not satisfy this.

The only unit-level tests target the exported PriceOrder algorithm; volume tiers and rounding are checked through PriceOrder rows, not by calling the unexported volumeDiscountPercent or percentOf directly. There are no tests of Checkout orchestration with a mocked or stubbed Store, and no standalone tests of trivial MemoryStore getters or the JSON mapping.

PriceOrder is tested with a table-driven t.Run test whose rows have descriptive names. The rows cover tier boundaries 9/10, 49/50 and 99/100 units, the coupon MinSubtotalCents boundary (equal applies), the MaxCouponDiscountCents cap (5000), the free-shipping threshold at exactly 7500 vs 7499 after the discount, and half-up rounding of a percentage.

Store is real (MemoryStore), with no hand-rolled mock or fake of the Store interface. Tests assert resulting state through store.Order / store.Product (e.g. an out-of-stock multi-line order leaves every line's stock unchanged, i.e. it is atomic) rather than counting Store calls. No test verifies calls on a stub or asserts the canned output of a double standing in for an in-process or managed collaborator.

ReceiptSender is the only replaced dependency, using a spy or mock that records the outgoing Receipt. Tests assert its To, OrderID and TotalCents on success. They also assert that no receipt is sent on failure paths, and that a failing sender still leaves the order persisted with ReceiptSent == false (201 with receipt_sent false).

Time is injected through svc.Now with a fixed instant, and the coupon expiry boundary is tested: now == ExpiresAt is rejected as ErrCouponExpired/422, while one instant earlier is accepted. NewID is injected or not asserted on. There is no time.Sleep and no real-clock dependence.

A plausible mutation is applied in a disposable copy (e.g. a tier `>=` changed to `>`, `!now.Before(c.ExpiresAt)` changed to `now.After(...)`, the stock check dropped, or the coupon cap removed). The report (saved under outputs/go-write-checkout/, or, only if the environment forbids writing report files and the answer says so, given complete inline) names the specific test that fails and confirms the original fixture is unmodified.

evals.name: go-refactor-brittle-signup-suite
evals.prompt: The Go package in evals/files/go/refactor-signup (user signup with e-mail verification: Service, MemoryUserStore, SHA256Hasher, HTTP handler) has a passing test suite in signup_test.go plus export_test.go. First, review the suite and give a findings list in which each finding names the specific tests involved and has a severity. Then refactor the suite. Keep production code unchanged, except where a test seam is strictly necessary; if you add one, state exactly what it is and why. Use only standard-library testing. The refactored suite must stay green: run it several times and with -race. Save the new test files, a diff of any production change, and the findings plus a before/after summary under outputs/go-refactor-signup/.
evals.expected_output: A findings list that names the planted anti-patterns (call-order and interaction verification on managed/in-process collaborators, assertions on stubs, reflection and export_test hooks, copy-pasted password tests, logic in tests, vague names, sleep/real clock) and the untested behaviors (duplicate registration through the real store, the HTTP handler). Then a green honeycomb-shaped suite: slice tests through NewHandler/Service with real MemoryUserStore and SHA256Hasher and a spy only for Mailer, plus one table test for CheckPassword.
expectations: The findings identify TestRegisterCallsCollaboratorsInOrder (the find/hash/save/send call log) and the findCalls/saveCalls/hashCalls counters in TestRegister1/TestRegister2 as interaction verification on managed or in-process collaborators (UserStore, Hasher). They explain that these break under behavior-preserving refactors, e.g. hashing before the lookup or replacing Find+Save with an insert that reports duplicates.

The findings identify assertions on stubs or on canned values from inappropriately substituted in-process/managed collaborators: store.lastFindEmail, u.PasswordHash == "hashed:Correct-Horse-9" (the mock's canned output), and duplicate detection 'tested' only through a canned findResult: true.
The findings flag reflection on the unexported tokens map in TestVerifyDeletesToken as implementation-detail testing.
The findings flag the export_test.go hooks NormalizeEmailForTest/BuildWelcomeMessageForTest and the exact-string TestWelcomeMessage as testing unexported internals.
The findings flag the conditional logic in TestNormalizeEmail that re-derives the expected value (logic in tests / computed expectation).
The findings flag the vague names TestRegister1, TestRegister2 and TestItWorks.
The findings flag the four copy-pasted TestPassword* tests that assert only Problems[0].
The findings flag time.Sleep with the real clock in TestTokenExpiry.

Findings carry severities consistent with the skill's review checklist: assertions on stubs and mocked managed dependencies (so real bugs pass) are high; call-count/call-order verification, reflection or private-member access, and sleeps with the real clock are at least medium; vague names and copy-paste are low.

The answer identifies the uncovered behavior: duplicate registration through the real MemoryUserStore (including case/whitespace variants such as " Bob@Example.com " after "bob@example.com") is never exercised, so the suite would stay green if MemoryUserStore.FindByEmail never found anything. It also notes that NewHandler (201/400/409 on signup, 204/400/410 on verify, 201 when the welcome mail fails) is entirely untested.

The refactored suite has a honeycomb shape. Feature tests use the real NewMemoryUserStore and the real SHA256Hasher and cover: register, then extract the token from the mailer spy, then verify so the user becomes Verified; reusing the token is rejected; a duplicate in any case/whitespace variant is rejected; and a Mailer failure still leaves the user registered.
The HTTP status mapping is tested through NewHandler with httptest: at least signup 201 and 409, and verify 204, 400 and 410 (410 is reachable with TokenTTL 0 and no production change).

Password enforcement stays covered through the feature entry point, not only through CheckPassword: at least one weak-password signup (through NewHandler with httptest, or Service.Register) asserts 400 (or a *WeakPasswordError), that no user was stored (e.g. MemoryUserStore.FindByEmail returns not found, or a later valid signup with the same email succeeds with 201), and that the Mailer spy recorded no email. Removing the CheckPassword call from Register must make this test fail; the detailed CheckPassword table is kept in addition.

Existing email-validation and password-hash coverage is preserved through the feature entry point. (a) At least two invalid addresses (e.g. "no-at-sign.com" and "x@nodot") are rejected through Service.Register (ErrInvalidEmail) or NewHandler (400), each asserting that no user was stored and that the Mailer spy recorded no email; removing the ErrInvalidEmail check from normalizeEmail must make this fail. (b) A successful registration, read back through the real MemoryUserStore, asserts the persisted PasswordHash equals an independently computed literal "sha256:<64 hex>" digest for a fixed password and a nonempty pepper (a literal, not computed by calling SHA256Hasher or sha256 in the test); a prefix-plus-length check alone does not satisfy this. Storing an empty, plaintext, constant, pepper-ignoring or otherwise malformed hash (e.g. "broken" or "sha256:" + 64 "x") must make this fail. These are separate from the weak-password requirement above.

Only Mailer is replaced with a test double (a spy asserting recipient, subject or a link containing the token). There are no mocks of UserStore or Hasher, no call-count or call-order assertions on them, no reflection on unexported fields (reflect.DeepEqual on returned values is fine), and the export_test.go hooks are removed or unused.

The four TestPassword* tests become one table-driven t.Run test of CheckPassword with descriptively named rows. The rows cover 9/10 and 72/73-byte boundaries, each missing character class, the local-part rule including the exemption for a local part under 3 bytes (the documented rule counts bytes), and multiple simultaneous violations, asserting the full problem list.

CheckPassword is the only unit-tested function. Email normalization is verified only through behavior (e.g. registering " Bob@Example.com " after "bob@example.com" returns 409/ErrEmailTaken), not by unit-testing the unexported normalizeEmail.

time.Sleep is removed and token expiry is tested deterministically: either through an injected clock seam (e.g. a Now func() time.Time field on Service defaulting to time.Now) that the answer explicitly declares as the only production change and justifies, or with no production change (e.g. TokenTTL 0 vs 1h), in which case the answer explicitly states that this still reads the real clock and leaves the exact expiry boundary (now == expires) untested, and names the clock seam as the fix. No other production code changes. The final suite passes with `go test -race -count=N ./...`.

Replacement tests are shown to catch a defect, not just claimed to: the answer gives a concrete production mutation applied only in a disposable copy (e.g. MemoryUserStore.FindByEmail made to never find a user, the token not deleted after Verify, or a CheckPassword length boundary shifted), the exact command run against that copy (e.g. `go test ./...` in the copy), and the name of the new behavioral test (or t.Run row) that failed. A bare statement that the new suite would catch it does not satisfy this.

evals.name: ts-write-checkout-suite
evals.prompt: Write a Vitest test suite for the supplied TypeScript checkout module (evals/files/ts/write-checkout). CheckoutService.placeOrder is the feature entry point; pricing.ts holds the pricing rules, store.ts is our own SQLite database (node:sqlite, ':memory:' works), and ports.ts has the clock, id source and the HttpOrderMailer that calls our third-party email provider. Leave production code unchanged. Work in a copy of the fixture, run npm install, npm test and npm run typecheck, then show the suite catches a plausible defect by mutating a disposable copy of the production code and running the suite against it. Save the test files under outputs/ts-write-checkout/test/ and a short outputs/ts-write-checkout/REPORT.md covering the test portfolio (what goes through placeOrder, what's unit-tested and why), which dependencies are real, faked or mocked, the commands you ran, and the mutation result.
evals.expected_output: A small honeycomb-shaped Vitest suite. Most tests go through CheckoutService.placeOrder with a real CheckoutStore on ':memory:' SQLite, an injected fixed Clock and deterministic IdSource, and a recording fake/spy for OrderMailer only. A small named-row table (it.each/test.for) covers the pricing boundaries. The suite passes, a disposable mutation is caught, and the report explains the portfolio and dependency choices.
expectations: Most feature behavior is tested by calling CheckoutService.placeOrder with real wiring and a real CheckoutStore.open(':memory:'), then asserting on the result and on persisted state read back through the store (for example getProduct(...).stock, getOrder(id), redemptionCount). At least one successful placeOrder test asserts exact literal stock balances read back through getProduct(...).stock afterwards (e.g. 10 -> 8 after buying 2), preferably for two or more lines with different quantities, so a decrement that does nothing (e.g. `stock - 0 * ?`) or hits the wrong SKU fails it. No test mocks, stubs or spies on CheckoutStore methods.

Unit tests are few and cover only the pricing algorithm (priceOrder/volumeDiscountPercent). As in the skill, 'few' and 'most' are judged by unit-tested units, test functions/tables and distinct behaviors covered, not by table-row count: one dense pricing boundary table whose rows outnumber the placeOrder tests is fine, as long as feature behaviors (stock, coupons, expiry, atomicity, email) are covered through placeOrder. There are no isolated unit tests of CheckoutService orchestration with mocked collaborators, and no tests of trivial code such as the store's row mapping or systemClock.

Pricing boundaries use one or more tables (it.each or test.for) with a descriptive name per row. The rows cover volume tier edges at quantity 9/10 and 49/50 exercised through priceOrder (or placeOrder), each row asserting the literal volumeDiscountCents and subtotal/total, so replacing volumeDiscountPercent(line.quantity) with 0 inside priceOrder fails the suite; rows that only call volumeDiscountPercent do not satisfy this. They also cover the free-shipping threshold at merchandise 4999 vs 5000 cents measured after the coupon, the coupon minSubtotalCents edge, and at least one rounding case (Math.round per line or Math.floor for the coupon). Differently shaped scenarios are not forced into the same table.

Clock and IdSource are injected as fixed or deterministic fakes, with no Date.now, real timers or sleeps. The coupon expiry edge is tested through placeOrder on both sides of validUntil, with 'now == validUntil' accepted and 1 ms later rejected with COUPON_EXPIRED, and exact order ids and createdAt values are asserted.

OrderMailer is the only test double that records interactions. It is a spy or fake whose assertions check the outgoing confirmation (to, orderId, totalCents, lines). A test also shows that a throwing mailer still leaves the order committed (getOrder returns it) and returns emailSent: false.

Through placeOrder and the real DB, at least one slice test checks atomicity: an OUT_OF_STOCK (or other failure) on a later line leaves the stock of earlier lines unchanged, stores no order and sends no email, so removing the ROLLBACK fails it. Coupon redemption is covered through placeOrder and the real DB in both directions: an eligible purchase with a coupon succeeds, stores the order with that couponCode and leaves redemptionCount at 1; the same customer's second use of that coupon is then rejected with COUPON_ALREADY_USED, leaves redemptionCount at 1, leaves stock unchanged from after the first order, stores no second order (getOrder for the next deterministic id is undefined) and sends no second email. So deleting recordRedemption fails a test. Global exhaustion is covered separately, because a same-customer retry is stopped by hasRedeemed before maxRedemptions is ever checked: a coupon is used up through successful purchases (e.g. maxRedemptions 1 and one purchase by customer A), then a different customer's attempt is rejected with COUPON_EXHAUSTED, with stock unchanged from after the last successful order, no new order stored, redemptionCount still equal to maxRedemptions, and no additional email, so removing the maxRedemptions check fails a test. A test that only shows a below-minSubtotalCents coupon is not redeemed does not satisfy this on its own. In addition, the 'only consume the coupon when it actually discounted the order' contract is covered through placeOrder and the real DB with two named rows: a subtotal below the coupon's minSubtotalCents, and an eligible subtotal whose Math.floor coupon discount rounds to 0 (e.g. percentOff 1 on a 99-cent subtotal). Each row asserts that placeOrder succeeds (ok: true) with quote.couponApplied false, that the stored order read back through getOrder has couponCode null, that redemptionCount for the coupon is unchanged (e.g. still 0), and that a later eligible purchase with the same coupon by the same customerId succeeds (ok: true, couponApplied true) rather than being rejected with COUPON_ALREADY_USED. Changing `if (coupon && quote.couponApplied)` to `if (coupon)` before recordRedemption must make these rows fail.

Quantity validation is covered through placeOrder and the real DB, not only through priceOrder: a named-row table rejects zero, negative, fractional (e.g. 1.5) and over-limit (1000, above MAX_QUANTITY_PER_LINE 999) quantities with reason INVALID_QUANTITY, and each row asserts literal stock unchanged, no order stored (getOrder for the next deterministic id is undefined), redemptionCount unchanged when the row supplies an eligible coupon, and no email sent. Removing the quantity guard in priceOrder must make this table fail (without it, a quantity of -2 increases stock and persists an order).
The suite passes under npm test and npm run typecheck (tsc --noEmit) against the unchanged fixture.

The report shows a disposable-copy mutation (for example a tier boundary changed from >= to >, a removed ROLLBACK, or a flipped expiry comparison) that makes a named test fail, and the original fixture is left untouched.

REPORT.md (or, only if the environment forbids writing report files and the answer says so, one complete report given inline; notes scattered across the message do not count) labels each dependency as real (SQLite store, pricing), faked (clock, ids) or mocked (mailer, as the unmanaged third-party boundary), explains why only pricing gets unit tests, and lists the commands run.

evals.name: ts-refactor-registration-suite
evals.prompt: Our Vitest suite for the event registration service (evals/files/ts/refactor-registration, test/registration.test.ts) passes but keeps breaking whenever we touch src/registration.ts and still lets bugs through. First review the suite: give a findings list that cites specific tests by name and explains the problem with each. Then refactor the suite. Keep production code unchanged unless a seam is strictly needed, and if you add one, say exactly what and why. The suite must stay green. Work in a copy, run npm install, npm test and npm run typecheck, and save the new test file(s) under outputs/ts-refactor-registration-suite/test/ plus outputs/ts-refactor-registration-suite/REVIEW.md with the findings, any production change, and the before/after test run output.
evals.expected_output: A findings list that names the planted anti-patterns: mocked managed repository with interaction checks, assertions on stubs, private-method access via `as any`, copy-pasted price tests, loop/conditional logic, vague names, a real clock and sleep, the brittle listRegistrations call-count test, and missing coverage of cancel() waitlist promotion. It is followed by a green suite that runs mostly through RegistrationService.register/cancel on a real InMemoryEventRepository with a controlled clock, a named-row table for the pricing tiers, and a Notifier spy as the only mock.
expectations: The review identifies 'calls repository correctly' as brittle under a behavior-preserving refactor. It notes that the test asserts listRegistrations was called exactly twice, that findEvent was called before listRegistrations, and that the private countConfirmed was spied on, so merging the duplicate listRegistrations call would fail the test even though behavior is unchanged.

The review flags that cancel() (freeing a confirmed seat promotes the earliest WAITLISTED registration to CONFIRMED and notifies them) has no coverage at all, and the refactored suite adds a test for it through the public API with at least two WAITLISTED attendees registered at distinct, controlled times (fake timers, a clock seam, or seeded registeredAt values).
